Chapter 2. The Slow Unraveling of Peace.
As the weeks go by, you can almost feel the cracks in Rwanda’s fragile peace getting wider. What starts as everyday routine for the mission soon turns unsettling—there’s an attack on a village here, a political meeting there that ends in shouts and chaos, even a radio broadcast laced with hate. On their own, these incidents might seem small. But, put together, they reveal a country quietly slipping toward disaster.
The peacekeepers find themselves constantly on the move, barely catching their breath as they jump from one crisis to the next. Government officials keep insisting everything’s just fine, while behind the scenes, it’s clear militias are quietly stockpiling weapons. Opposition leaders, meanwhile, are sounding the alarm—pleading for protection, warning anyone who’ll listen that worse is coming. Every mission report feels more urgent than the last, but outside help? It’s slow, cautious, and hesitant.
Then, one day, a young officer comes back from patrol visibly shaken. He talks about a village he visited—houses burned to the ground, people missing. The local police brush it off as a simple land dispute, but he’s not buying it. He can’t forget the fear in the eyes of the few who survived, or shake the feeling that something far darker is unfolding.
Inside the mission, leaders are struggling to piece things together. The rules they’ve been handed seem clear... but the situation in front of them is anything but. Should they push for stronger action, even if it means putting their own people at risk? The sense of helplessness in the room is impossible to ignore.
Out in the markets and on the streets, life tries to go on. There’s a mother hurrying her children home before dark, constantly glancing at groups of young men on the corners. A teacher worries about reopening the school—what if her students become targets? Everywhere you look, tension hangs in the air, shaping every little choice.
Meanwhile, the world outside seems far away—caught up in other crises, and hesitant to get involved here. The mission keeps sending out urgent messages, warning that things are spiraling. The replies? Polite, but vague—requests for more details, promises to review the situation, but never anything concrete.
One evening, a local journalist sits down and shares something that hits hard—a friend taken from his home in the middle of the night. No one knows where he is, and the police refuse to help. You can hear the fear in the journalist’s voice as he talks about the growing list of missing people, about the dread that’s taken hold of the city. For many, the violence isn’t just a looming threat—it’s already become part of daily life.
Inside the mission, the mood gets heavier. The peacekeepers are exhausted, stretched thin, starting to wonder if any of it is making a difference. The feeling of isolation grows, as if the rest of the world has simply turned its back on Rwanda.
And even as the evidence of danger piles up, the rules don’t change. The peacekeepers are told: observe, report, but don’t step in. You can feel the frustration, the anger, the despair. The world’s promises of “never again” suddenly seem hollow—little comfort for people living right on the edge of catastrophe.
